analysis.one_liner: Ends federal marijuana prohibition and replaces it with federal excise taxes, licensing, and regulation.
analysis.headline: Sen. Wyden's bill to end federal marijuana prohibition and tax it like alcohol drew zero cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 30, 2017, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove marijuana from the federal list of controlled substances, ending federal criminal penalties for possessing, growing, and selling it. In its place, it would set up a system like the one used for alcohol: licensed producers and importers, federal excise taxes that start at 10% of the sales price and climb to 25%, a $1,000-a-year tax on every production site, and strict rules on packaging, labels, and advertising. States could still ban marijuana within their borders, and shipping it into a state where it is illegal would remain a crime.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use, grow, or sell marijuana would no longer face federal criminal prosecution, and states with legal marijuana programs would get a clear federal framework instead of a patchwork of guidance. Anyone worried about federal drug enforcement would benefit from the elimination of federal marijuana trafficking penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marijuana users, growers, and state-legal businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Attorney General to remove marijuana from all schedules of the Controlled Substances Act within 60 days of enactment, ending federal criminal penalties for marijuana [S2][S3].

It strikes the federal criminal penalties for marijuana distribution and import/export offenses from the Controlled Substances Act, so no one could be federally prosecuted for marijuana activity alone [S3].

It would replace the Drug Enforcement Administration's marijuana enforcement role with the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau and ATF, treating marijuana like alcohol rather than like a dangerous drug [S2][S3].
It gives FDA the same authority over marijuana it has over alcohol, creating consumer protections on labeling, advertising, and product claims [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay a federal excise tax on every marijuana product, starting at 10% of the sales price and rising to 25% within five years. Producers, importers, and warehouse operators would pay permit fees, post bonds covering their tax liability, pay a $1,000 annual occupational tax per site, and bear the cost of meeting federal recordkeeping, packaging, and labeling rules.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax reaches 25% of the sales price within four years, and afterward is set at roughly 25% of the prevailing market price per ounce, which would keep legal marijuana expensive relative to untaxed illegal products [S3].

Applicants with a marijuana-related felony conviction in the previous five years can be denied a federal permit, so people with past convictions — the very people most harmed by prohibition — could be barred from the newly legal industry [S3].
The permit, bond, and recordkeeping requirements mirror the alcohol industry's structure, which historically favors large, well-financed companies over small operators [S3].
Retail sales would be capped at one ounce per transaction, with fines up to $10,000 and up to five years in prison for violations, and states could keep marijuana fully illegal [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending federal prohibition is a substantial gain for ordinary people: it eliminates federal criminal exposure for millions and replaces an enforcement regime with a tax and regulatory one. The main costs are financial — a steep excise tax passed to consumers and compliance burdens on businesses — plus a real equity flaw in denying permits to people with recent marijuana convictions. The design is workable but heavy-handed, modeled on alcohol regulation rather than built for the existing state-legal market.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill and it went straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or brought it up, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Marijuana Revenue and Regulation Act on March 30, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
No cosponsor ever signed onto the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won: federal prohibition of marijuana continued, and the illicit market and existing enforcement apparatus faced no new tax or competition. Consumers and would-be legal businesses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal prohibition and the illicit market

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; it was referred to the Finance Committee, where he is a senior member.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, a markup, or a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no partisan split is recorded; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would turn state-legal marijuana businesses into federally licensed enterprises, locking in a permitted, taxed production system modeled on alcohol. The trade-off for the public is legal access and consumer protections, but the steep excise tax and permit requirements would raise prices and tend to favor well-capitalized firms.

A federal legal, taxed market would undercut illegal sellers who charge prohibition-inflated prices and operate with no consumer protections. The bill keeps penalties for shipping into states where marijuana is illegal, preserving some room for enforcement.

industries.industry: Federal drug enforcement and private prisons
industries.note: Removing marijuana from the controlled substances lists would eliminate federal marijuana prosecutions and transfer enforcement away from the DEA, reducing demand for drug enforcement work and incarceration.
